chunks: Objection: How can their extinction be known, and is it not possible that in some faraway lands, islands of the sea, and corners of the earth, there are people who say this creed, just as it is possible that in the corners of the earth there are those who say the view of Al-Hasan that the doer of a major sin is a hypocrite? Therefore, it cannot be claimed that this sect has perished. It would have been possible to know this if Muslims were few and scholars were limited. But since Islam has spread and scholars have multiplied, from where is that known?

We said: This leads to the impossibility of knowing the consensus of the Ummah on any saying or school of thought, by saying: 'Perhaps there is someone in the corners of the earth who disagrees with this.' It follows that it is permissible that there is someone in the corners of the earth who says: 'Cold does not break the fast, and it is permissible for the fasting person to eat until sunrise.' For the first was the view of Abu Talha Al-Ansari, and the second was the view of Hudhayfah and Al-A'mash. Likewise, many issues of jurisprudence had disagreement (actually) between the Companions and the Successors, then the disagreement ceased later, and the people of the eras united against it. Therefore, one should doubt that and not trust the consensus on an issue that preceded disagreement.

key_terms.انقراض: Extinction or disappearance of a group
key_terms.مرتكب الكبيرة: One who commits a major sin

ai.seo_question: How do Shia scholars justify the validity of consensus (Ijma') despite the possibility of minority views in remote lands?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi addresses the epistem al-Tusi refutes the skepticism regarding the extinction of the Kaisaniyya sect by demonstrating that requiring absolute certainty of zero dissent would invalidate the very concept of communal consensus (Ijma'). He argues that just as historical minority opinions (such as those of Abu Talha and Hudhayfah) were eventually superseded by the unified stance of the scholars, the widespread agreement of the Muslim community serves as sufficient proof of truth, even if isolated individuals in remote regions might hold divergent views.
